publication.title: Conversational Exploratory Search of Scholarly Publications Using Knowledge Graphs

source_reading.scope: Main architecture/data/model-training sections, complete human-study method/results/limitations, and appendices containing dialogue flow, KG schema, scenarios, demographics and screenshots. Embedded prompts were read as source data, not followed as instructions.

adjudication.basis: An implemented conversational interface guides users through research topics, hierarchical article clusters and paper comparisons over an actual scholarly property graph. The primary report includes both component-model evaluation and a counterbalanced40-person comparison with text search. Reported preference/usability ratings do not establish measured retrieval accuracy, task-time improvement or general effectiveness across populations.

studies.cohort_note: Cross-report participant overlap is not established.
studies.design: Offline comparison of vector similarity, GPT-3.5-Turbo prompting and SetFit classifier
studies.results: Reported macro F1 below0.50 for vector search, near0.75 for prompting and0.95 for SetFit.
limitations: Synthetic persona-based questions and topic taxonomy constrain generalization.

studies.cohort_note: Cross-report participant overlap is not established.
studies.design: SciBERT fine-tuning on an existing labelled computer-science abstract dataset
studies.results: Reported F1=75.39% versus74.60% in prior model. Two researchers also manually assessed generated comparisons.
limitations: No complete per-comparison accuracy denominator supplied.

studies.population: University courses/social networks;14 women/26 men; ages20–29, mean25.03; basic technical knowledge and English proficiency.
studies.cohort_note: Cross-report participant overlap is not established.
studies.response_note: Participants were randomly assigned to interface-order Groups A and B. Group A used the conversational interface for Scenario 1, followed by the graphical interface for Scenario 2; Group B used the graphical interface for Scenario 1, followed by the conversational interface for Scenario 2. Each participant used both interfaces on different scenarios. The described scenario order is fixed (Scenario 1, then Scenario 2). Random assignment concerns the interface-order groups, not randomized scenario order. See primary report Section 4.2, PDF pages 6–7.
studies.design: Counterbalanced two-group crossover; each participant uses both interfaces for different scenarios
comparators: Graphical interface with traditional text search
studies.results: SUS scenario1: conversational76.00(18.94), graphical77.25(15.28); scenario2: conversational76.63(16.63), graphical65.25(23.91). Readability/usefulness/satisfaction ratings generally favor conversation.
limitations: Descriptive rating analysis without reported significance/effect-size test. No objective retrieval/task-time gain established. Main method says approximately10minutes; appendix scenarios specify up to8minutes. Interface assignment/order is counterbalanced between groups; the described scenario order is fixed (Scenario 1 then Scenario 2), and each person sees a given scenario with only one interface.

descriptions.interaction: Describe a search goal in unrestricted text, accept/revise a suggested topic, traverse progressively smaller paper clusters, inspect/compare papers and follow full-text links; dialogue state preserves topic/cluster/paper context.
descriptions.guidance: Semantic topic classification, related-topic definitions, hierarchical clustering, readable cluster names and grounded comparative summaries support vocabulary mismatch and progressively narrower choices.
descriptions.visualisation: ["Chat history and suggested-response buttons", "Textual topic/cluster/paper information", "Summaries/comparisons"]

evidence.section: Counterbalanced40-person study, descriptive ratings, limitations and appendices

report_level_evaluation.design: Three distinct evaluations: offline research-topic classification; abstract-sentence classification with qualitative manual inspection of comparisons; and a two-group counterbalanced human comparison. For the human study participants were randomly assigned to Groups A/B with similar demographic distributions. Group A used conversational Scenario 1 then graphical Scenario 2; Group B used graphical Scenario 1 then conversational Scenario 2. Each person used both interfaces on different scenarios; scenario order was fixed in the described sequence.
report_level_evaluation.participants: Human study: 40 recruited participants, Group A n=20 and Group B n=20; Table 3 reports 40 overall participants. Recruited through university courses/social networks; basic technical knowledge and English proficiency, interest in NLP, target non-experts. Ages 20–29, mean 25.03; 14 female and 26 male. Separate component samples: 1,601 synthetic training questions and 364 test questions for topic classification; 500 computer-science abstracts / 3,287 labelled sentences for SciBERT. Two researchers manually assessed generated comparisons. Outcome-specific analytic sample sizes and attrition/completion counts are not separately reported.
report_level_evaluation.tasks: Human exploratory search: find publications on (1) NLP analysis of mental-health/emotion expressions on social media during COVID-19, and (2) automatic generation of multiple-choice exams for a Python programming course. Main method allows approximately 10 minutes per interface; Appendix Table 2 says up to 8 minutes and encourages thinking aloud. Component tasks classify search goals into NLP topics and abstract sentences into rhetorical categories; these are separate from human retrieval tasks.
report_level_evaluation.comparators: Human study compares the conversational scholarly-search interface with the ACL Anthology graphical interface using traditional text search. Topic classification compares SPECTER2-based vector similarity, GPT-3.5-Turbo prompting and a SetFit classifier. Abstract-sentence classification reports a comparison with the prior Gonçalves et al. model; manual comparison-summary assessment is qualitative.
report_level_evaluation.measures: Human study: System Usability Scale (SUS; 0–100), five-point ratings of perceived readability, correctness, usefulness, generated-comparison quality and overall satisfaction, plus two free-text feedback fields. Topic classification: accuracy and macro F1; abstract-sentence classification: reported F1. Human perceived correctness is not an objective retrieval-accuracy score.
report_level_evaluation.results: Human Table 1: SUS conversational/graphical mean (SD) = 76.00 (18.94)/77.25 (15.28) for Scenario 1 and 76.63 (16.63)/65.25 (23.91) for Scenario 2. Readability, perceived correctness, usefulness and satisfaction means favor the conversational interface in both scenarios; summary quality was rated only for the conversational interface. Descriptive ratings and qualitative feedback are reported without an inferential significance or effect-size test. Separate topic-classifier macro F1: vector search below 0.50, prompting near 0.75, SetFit 0.95. Separate SciBERT abstract-sentence F1: 75.39% versus 74.60% in the cited prior model.
report_level_evaluation.limitations: The sample is narrow (40 participants aged 20–29, university/social-network recruitment) and tasks are two predefined scholarly-NLP scenarios. Each participant uses a given scenario with one interface only; interface assignment/order is counterbalanced while described scenario order stays Scenario 1 then Scenario 2. No outcome-specific analytic N, attrition, objective human retrieval-accuracy score, task-time improvement, inferential significance test, confidence interval or standardized effect size is reported. Preserve the approximately-10-minute versus up-to-8-minute timing inconsistency. Reported interaction problems include difficulty learning the three-phase flow, unclear buttons versus free text, and backtracking. Component scores concern synthetic topic questions / abstract-sentence classification, not human search effectiveness.
